query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Replacing full ab initio thermodynamic integration with a two‐phase coexistence simulation driven by a machine‐learned interatomic potential will yield melting properties (melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and the volume change at melting) of refractory materials (e.g., high‐entropy refractory alloys) that are comparably accurate to DFT-based predictions but computed at a fraction of the cost.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-melting material (for example, a single-phase high-entropy alloy such as NbMoTaW) characterized by its high melting point and complex electronic and atomic disorder features.
generation.intervention: Develop and employ a machine‐learned potential (e.g., neural network or Gaussian approximation potential) trained on a limited set of DFT data, and use it to run two‐phase coexistence molecular dynamics simulations instead of full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed near the expected melting point under ambient pressure, with sufficiently large simulation cells to accommodate both solid and liquid phases, using the microcanonical ensemble to monitor phase fluctuations.
generation.structural_mediator: The solid–liquid interface present in the two‐phase simulation, which mediates atomic rearrangements and free-energy differences between the phases.
generation.mechanism: The machine‐learned potential, once adequately trained, reproduces key energetic and structural features of the material as predicted by DFT. In the two‐phase coexistence simulation, the system naturally equilibrates at the melting point, allowing direct estimation of the melting temperature and associated latent properties (entropy, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change) from the discontinuities in energy and density across the interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: The computed melting properties will be within an acceptable error margin (e.g., ~5–10% relative deviation) of high-fidelity DFT predictions and experimental observations, while reducing computational expense sufficiently to allow high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
generation.baseline: Traditional ab initio free-energy calculations employing full thermodynamic integration with DFT-based molecular dynamics simulations.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to work well for materials where a high-quality machine‐learned potential can be created; for systems with extremely complex bonding or where training data is scarce, the method’s accuracy may degrade.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding how accurately the machine‐learned potential will capture the subtle free energy differences near melting for multi-component refractory systems, and the error margins may depend on the quality and diversity of the DFT training set.

falsification_experiment.design: Choose a high-melting refractory material (such as NbMoTaW) for which experimental melting properties (melting point, latent heats, and volume change at melting) are available. Develop a machine‐learned potential trained on a modest DFT data set and run two‐phase (coexistence) MD simulations to determine the melting properties. Independently, perform high-fidelity DFT-based thermodynamic integration for the same material. Compare both simulation results against experimental values.
measurements: Melting temperature from the abrupt energy/density change in the simulation
Calculated enthalpy and entropy changes from the free-energy discontinuity at the interface
Volume change at melting from density differences between the solid and liquid phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two-phase machine-learned potential simulations predict melting properties that deviate significantly (e.g., more than ~10–15% off) from both high-fidelity DFT results and experimental data, then the method does not sufficiently replace full ab initio approaches for high-throughput melting property predictions.
